speechtext:
I can only answer the question fully by going extensively into the situation regarding the production of aircraft. This question was covered before by my colleague the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe), in a statement in the house on February 16, in so far as the production by A.V. Roe Canada Limited is concerned.
In answer to the hon. member for Nanaimo, I can tell him that we have today six squadrons of Sabre fighters abroad, the most formidable fighter aircraft in operation today. The importance of the Canadian Sabre squadrons was indicated by references to them in the press growing out of the recent incidents in Europe. Three more squadrons are on their way over. We shall complete our full commitment of an air division of twelve squadrons to NATO by the date set and we shall do that in the belief- which I think is shared by all Canadians- that the best place to defend Canada and to prevent aggression is as far away from our shores as possible.
As I have indicated, a report on the production of the CF-100 has already been made to the house-that is the other fighter aircraft we have in production-and this report and others available to me on the production of the aircraft and the engines
3340	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry indicate that it should be possible for us similarly to complete the planned build-up of our defences in Canada with these allweather fighters designed particularly to do that job. It was not possible to do this before because the aircraft with which to do it did not exist anywhere in the world. Had we gone into production of any earlier type we would have had a major part of our productive capacity engaged in producing planes which were either already obsolescent or which were not suited for the purpose. Instead of that we engaged in producing the CF-100 which is believed to be the leading long-range all-weather fighter aircraft, and it is specially designed, equipped and qualified to meet the needs of Canadian defence.
At all times during the past year and a half we have had a number of squadrons of Sabres for our defence pending their transfer to the other side, and we have had a large number of aircrew and aircraft in the operational training units. Exercise Signpost last July was the first major demonstration and exercise of air defence.
There is nothing new in the situation and it has been made plain from time to time. In "Canada's Defence Program" the white paper I put before parliament last session, in June, 1952, and which was widely distributed, I referred to the air defence of Canada; and after mentioning radar installations and communications I said:
At the same time fighter defence in Canada, both regular and reserve, is being built up. At present the fighter squadrons for this purpose are equipped with Vampire and Mustang aircraft. These will be replaced1 by CF-lOO's as they become available. In addition, there are a number of squadrons equipped with F-86E's and designated for the NATO air force in Europe. In the meantime they are available for the defence of this continent.
The statement then made was completely in accordance with the facts as they then existed and it has been amplified and repeated time after time ever since. It has been made perfectly plain that the first squadron of CF-lOO's was in process of formation. We could not establish it- equipped with this first all-weather long-range fighter to meet Canadian needs-until the planes were produced, and there were no suitable planes in production anywhere else.
Mr. Speaker, I have referred to the production -of F-86's and CF-lOO's. As to the production of F-86's, there may be some people still who are sorry that we did not take their advice and go into production on some other types of fighters which are now obsolete. I do not believe that the Royal


Air Force of the United Kingdom, which is receiving a large number of these fighters, would take that view. I do not believe that the United States Air Force, to which we sold a number of these fighters for use in Korea, would take that view.	I do not
believe that the countries of NATO and Britain, which are now being defended in part by our fighters abroad, would take that view either.	I do not believe that the
people of Canada would take that view because the F-86E and its production have been magnificent successes and major contributions to our combined defence.
Similarly, a year from now I believe that we shall look back on our decision to make the CF-100 and the Orenda engine in Canada as a major contribution to the defence of North America and of Canada itself.

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. I sent him last night a press clipping and notice of my question for today. It is this. In view of the fact that the Canadian ambassador to Colombia, Edmond Turcotte, indicated this week that Canada eventually might join the Pan-American Union if the union tendered such an invitation, will the Prime Minister tell the house whether the government has any steps in this direction in contemplation at the moment and whether that statement accurately reflects Canadian government policy?
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): The Department of External Affairs has no information other than the press report to which the hon. member for Peel refers about a statement attributed to the newly-appointed ambassador to Colombia concerning Canada's attitude to the organization of American states.
The position of the government of Canada in this respect has not changed since I last referred to this subject on February 12, 1949, when I spoke at a press conference in Washington. Speaking of the Organization of American States, formerly known as the Pan-American Union, I said:
Our government has been giving thought to the Pan-American Union over a great many years and our relations with the members of the Pan-American Union have always been most satisfactory. The angle from which this has been examined is as to whether our actual participation in the PanAmerican Union would be productive of any real advantage for any of its members. Our cultural, our trade relations, with other members of the Pan-American Union have always been very good and they will improve constantly. So far it has not appeared to us that there would be any decided advantage in a formal membership in the PanAmerican Union.

Estimated amount required to recoup the agricultural prices support account to cover the net operating loss of the agricultural prices support board during the fiscal year 1952-53, including authority to credit to the account the net revenue received into the agricultural products board account from the sale of New Zealand meat received in exchange for beef shipped to the United Kingdom, $32,346,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I can, Mr. Chairman. The Minister of Agriculture could not be present today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
First, with respect to hogs, on April 1, 1952, the agricultural prices support board held 5,492,520 pounds of canned pork produced to their specifications and had a further 92,768,454 pounds produced to their specifications up to March 31, 1953. It is estimated that by March 31 the board will have resold 25 million pounds of canned pork, principally in the domestic market, at a net loss to the board of $6,075,000. Various pork cut programs involving 101,437,581 pounds of product have been carried out and it is estimated that about 10 million pounds of these cuts will remain on hand as at March 31, 1953. The total loss on the cuts resold to March 31 is estimated at $2,738,828.08, which is mainly represented oy the payment of certain storage, transportation and other handling charges which
Supply-Agriculture
had to be added to the fresh cost in calculating the net loss.
Then, I presume the hon. member would like to have similar information with respect to cattle. In this connection the major .program has been one of acceptance of carcass beef for shipment to the United Kingdom in return for which New Zealand beef has been sold in the United States to offset the cost of the Canadian beef. Other programs have included the purchase of live cattle and the operation of the Canadian Co-operative Processors' plant at Swift Current, Saskatchewan, the acceptance of some boneless beef and carcass beef which are presently stored in Canada, and the acceptance of some specially prepared boneless beef which has been resold to the Department of National Defence for use by Canadian and commonwealth troops in Korea.
Up to March 31, 1953, it is estimated the board will have purchased 159,533 cattle and accepted product in the form of carcass and boneless beef as well as some live cattle. As at March 31, 1953, the board estimates it will hold in storage in Canada product equivalent to 38,555 cattle including those held alive on community pasture. About two-thirds of these cattle are stored in the form of frozen carcass beef and most of the balance in the form of boneless manufacturing beef. No cattle have been purchased since the lifting of the American embargo on March 1, 1953.
The board exported 70,210,913 pounds of carcass beef, the equivalent of 112,410 cattle, to the United Kingdom at a cost of $31,384,000. For purposes of establishing the net loss on this operation to March 31, 1953, estimated revenue from the sale of New Zealand beef received in exchange for the beef shipped to the United Kingdom has been used as an offset in the amount of $8,377,595, this operation resulting in a loss of $23,006,405 in the beef account. As there are still some intergovernmental arrangements to be finalized in connection with a part of this program, some further minor adjustments may be necessary in this account, but these will be adjusted in a final audited statement and presented for approval when the board makes its recoup vote for 1953-54, at the end of the following fiscal year.
The board accepted 1,505,647 pounds of boneless beef in the buffer zone area which the board has had canned, and sold the bulk of this product to Greece with a small quantity being sold in the Canadian market. The net loss on this product was $588,988.92. Some 812 cattle were bought and resold live at approximately cost, and the board is still

I do not suppose my hon. friend wants me to endeavour from memory to explain the rather complicated formula on which we make these grants to municipalities. Generally speaking, in order to obtain any grant under the general section the value of federal property in the municipality must exceed 4 per cent of the total assessed property in the municipality, and then 75 per cent of the excess is eligible for tax grant on the usual basis.
In addition we pay local improvement taxes, and then in addition where property is acquired from a municipality there is a tapering down transitional grant under a section of the Municipal Grants Act which permits payment of municipal taxes on a reducing scale over a period of a certain number of years, I think it is three or four years, and then it goes into the general fund.

I want to take but a moment of the committee's time in connection with this item. I have come to the very strong conviction with respect to the question of the relationship between the federal government and municipalities, particularly where there is a concentration of federal properties in that municipality, that some new arrangements should be made with respect to the payment of taxes by the federal authorities. That fact has been largely borne in upon some of us because Toronto township particularly has been experiencing considerable financial difficulties which are perhaps to be expected in the changing conditions that they find there. It seems to me that at the present time there is not very much justification really for the federal government not being

Supply-Finance
a taxpayer in the municipal field the same as anybody else. I know the minister has had arguments from time to time that seemed convincing at that time, but when they are applied practically I do not think they are very convincing at all.
I make this appeal to the minister and suggest to him that there should be some change in the legislation governing the relationship of the federal and municipal jurisdictions. You see what is happening in some of these places. Your department is charging the municipalities excise taxes on what they buy and at the same time you are not paying your share of taxes in the municipal field. I know that is a bald statement and perhaps oversimplifies the problem, and I have no desire to do that. I do want to point out to the minister, however, that in our own province-and perhaps it applies to other provinces as well-they have made themselves available for taxation by the municipalities. I can remember a year ago, when that was done in Ontario by act of the legislature, asking the minister if we were going to do that in the federal field, and the minister said, no, it was not the policy of the government at that time to do it.
I do not want to be unduly critical in this thing, but I am convinced in my own mind that it is the wrong principle to follow, and I have taken the opportunity of this discussion at this time to impress it again upon the minister. I think the whole thing should be reviewed, and there should be at least some classification, if you like, of federal property. It may be that there are some federal properties, although none come to my mind, that should not be taxed by the municipalities. Perhaps there are some instances, but the minister would know more about that than I do. The municipalities have to bear such a tremendous load now that in many instances they are unable to do it. Some review should be made of the legislation, and I ask the minister at this time to do it. I do not want to take up any more of the time of the committee discussing this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend. As he knows, the present system was suggested to the house only after a great deal of study. It represented the best judgment we could exercise as to what should be done. I call the attention of the committee to the fact that it is the first time in the history of Canada since confederation that any federal government has attempted to pay anything in the way of municipal taxes to municipalities.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; no preceding government has ever attempted to do it. It was always stoutly resisted. We did work it out. It may be possible that the formula can be improved, but nevertheless it was arrived at after a great deal of careful study and, in my present view, represented a very great advance over what had existed before, and is reasonably fair. I do not suggest it is the last word, and I think perhaps we may continue to examine it; but it has provided a considerable measure of assistance to a great many municipalities where there was excessive concentration of federal property. But we can look into it again.

I should like to say to the minister that it was a step in the right direction, but I should also like to urge upon him the necessity of giving further consideration to this matter. I have in mind a very small municipality in my own constituency where the Department of National Defence expropriated a good part of the land for a bombing range. We were very glad to have that bombing range, but it made it extremely difficult for this small township to carry on. There is one other thing I should add to that. There are very many heavy vehicles travelling over the roads in that small township, and the township had to spend a considerable amount of money to try to keep up the roads. The Department of National Defence did make some small grant to that municipality to help it to maintain the roads. What I wanted to say particularly this afternoon was that the minister should give further consideration to this matter and endeavour to give some assistance to the smaller municipalities because of the fact that years ago the dominion government did not own nearly so much property as it owns today, and it is making it more difficult each year for some of the municipalities to carry on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I am not quite sure what my hon. friend wishes me to say. It is clear that all three levels of government-federal, provincial and local-have problems in raising the necessary money to defray the costs of the services their people demand. The municipalities undoubtedly have difficulty. I sympathize with the councils of municipalities who have to raise these moneys, because I know something of the problem, myself. Having to raise funds necessary to pay federal expenditures, I have known the problem for a long time.
The municipalities are the creatures of the provinces, as we know. They can obtain from the provinces such taxing powers as those provinces see fit to confer upon them within the constitutional limits imposed by the provinces. I have always felt it was improper that there should be direct financial discussion between the federal government and the municipalities because, as I have said,
Supply-Finance
the municipalities derive their power from and are the creatures of the provinces. Any discussion as to financial requirements of municipalities must, in the first and every instance, be directed to the legislative body which brings them into existence. Then in the discussions which take place from time to time between the provincial and federal governments it is quite proper of course to take into account all those discussions concerning the requirements of the junior taxing bodies in the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The $532,715 is required for the current year contribution, and really represents an underestimation in the main estimates. The additional amount required is due primarily to some salary increases, and more particularly to the fact that there are a number of civil servants who have been given permanent status during the year, and therefore a larger amount is required for the current government contribution.
Then, as to the status of the fund itself, perhaps the committee would like me to give a brief review of the situation as it is at the moment. At December 31, 1947, the total

Supply-Finance
estimated liability was $341,149,000 and the balance in the accounts amounted to $89,544,000, leaving a deficit of $251,605,000. By December 31,	1951, the deficit had
increased to an estimated $312,000,000, even after a special contribution in the amount of $75,000,000 had been made.
This deficit position was carefully studied in order to determine what should be done to reduce it and to prevent the creation of a new one. The deficit had been caused almost entirely by two main factors. First, the government had only matched contributions of employees for their current service and not those for their prior service and, secondly, since the contribution rates are calculated on the basis of a normal progression up the established salary scales, when there is a general salary increase, the contributions already made are actually inadequate in relation to the larger pension which will be received.
I indicated that the government proposed to continue the policy initiated at the close of 1950-51 to wipe out the accumulated deficit by means of bulk contributions over a reasonable period, and in order that the causes of that deficit would not continue to have effect I indicated my intention to show on the government balance sheet the full estimated actuarial liability of the superannuation fund at the end of each fiscal year and to credit to the account each year thereafter an amount equal to interest reckoned at 4 per cent calculated on the amount of the full actuarial liability of the fund rather than on the actual balance in the fund.
In the final supplementary estimates last year, I included an item to make up for the portion of the deficit related to past service contributions which had not been matched. A further item was included in those estimates to match the increase in the net liability of the fund which was created by the general salary increase, effective December 1, 1951, and finally a third item in those estimates constituted a bulk contribution to further write down the existing deficit. These contributions reduced the outstanding deficit in the account to $214,000,000 as of March 31, 1952.
Reference to the public accounts for 1951-52 will indicate quite clearly to hon. members that the policy which I announced last year at this time is being followed.
Item 571 in the estimates now before us is simply a further bulk contribution designed to reduce the outstanding deficit in the account from $214,000,000 to $189,000,000.

The items on the page include $177,000 for the lieutenant governors. If you subtract that, you arrive at my figure. It is just a question, Mr. Chairman, whether that is not a little too large a sum for this establishment.
I know that comparisons are always difficult to make, and this one may be a bit embarrassing; but I cannot help but compare what it costs for us to maintain the Governor General and his residence with what we pay to the Prime Minister and the maintenance of his residence. It is a much smaller figure. I believe there is $23,000 altogether in salaries and allowances, and $25,000 for the maintenance of that house. We are in a rather awkward position. The Governor General is the titular head of the country, yet he is appointed on the recommendation of the Prime Minister who is the political leader of the country. There seems to be a great difference between the $25,000 for the maintenance of one establishment and the $228,000 for the maintenance of the other establishment. I hear people say that the Prime Minister does not have to entertain, but I understand he does have to do a certain amount of entertaining.
The suggestion was made that the Governor General should not be required to dip into his own funds. We pay him this salary of $48,667, which is not subject to income tax, although it has been pointed out that he pays income tax on his own private income. Now, the Prime Minister says that there have been few changes in the total amount we have paid for this establishment since 1914. I have not the books before me to look up the figures for the various years that far back. I am interested, however, in the figures for the year ending March 31, 1952. The amount requested by the Minister of Finance for the Governor General at that time represented a slight reduction. In other words, in that year apparently some effort was made to cut down the total amount being spent for this establishment, and there was a reduction in this very item we are now discussing of $2,468 as compared with the 1950-51 fiscal year. It seems strange that it was possible, just two or three years ago, to apply the concept of economy and pare things down a bit at government house, but now we are told that there has been this substantial increase of $50,000. I understand that this increase is in relation to the allowances for

the purchase of goods, the hiring of help and so on. You have to look at that in relation to what was spent on allowances before. The amount before was $50,000, so it is not just a little increase in proportion to the current rise in the cost of living, it is actually a doubling of that amount. The Minister of Finance has had a fair amount to say about this item that is now before us being comparable to the item in the main estimates. May I point out that the item in the main estimates is, in effect, the beginning of a new policy of paying $100,000 of allowances instead of $50,000. This policy does not begin until the start of the new fiscal year on April 1. We are now being called upon to make this increase retroactive to last April 1. Frankly, I wonder whether there is not room, even with all the respect that we have for the office and the respect and regard we have for the person who occupies the office, for the kind of economy approach that was tried back in 1951-52, rather than this substantial increase.

Mr. Chairman, I do not rise to object to this item. I must say that I do not altogether agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. When we consider that the Governor General represents the sovereign in this country, and when we realize the tremendous expense the sovereign must be to the people of England-to which I understand we make no contribution-I think the contribution which we in this country make to the Governor General is certainly not out of line for a country of our size and wealth.
My understanding from what the Prime Minister said is that it is costing us $5,000 a month more for the upkeep of the present Governor General that it did in the past; that is $60,000 a year. In his remarks he said he thought the Canadian people would wish to pay this amount in order to maintain the standard which we, as a great country, should have.
I should like to say that I feel the Canadian people should have been ashamed of the niggardly fashion in which they have treated governors general in the past. It seems to me that if we have been paying $60,000 too little in the past to our governors general, it is time we were bringing that position up to the standard of a country like Canada.

I was aware, in a general way, that the situation was difficult before Lord Alexander retired, but I did not know what the actual figures were. When the situation was brought to our attention some months ago, it was gone into, and I can assure hon. members that it was very carefully checked because we were not at all

anxious to have to bring before parliament any recommendations for the change in the allowances that were made just after there had been a change in the incumbent of that high office. The officials went into the figures very carefully with the comptroller. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre feels that there could be economies made, and that was looked into. It was found that in the actual expenditures, there did not seem to be any item that could be dispensed with without changing the scale on which the responsibilities of representing the sovereign were discharged in Canada.
This being the situation, it was felt that this recommendation should be made. The hon. member says there is a difference between the expenses there and the expenses of the house provided for the Prime Minister. Well, there is a very substantial difference in the size of the two establishments and the number of personnel required for their proper upkeep. All of that does have to be taken into account.
And the office work is done at Rideau Hall.

This amount does not only provide living accommodation for government house, it also provides for the whole administrative branch of the Governor General's office. In addition to the amounts that are required for the upkeep of 24 Sussex street, there are offices supplied to me here in the central block, there are offices supplied in the east block and there is personnel supplied to assist me in the discharge of my duties. The hon. member for Royal is quite right. This is an extremely modest sum when compared with the substantial sums that have to be provided out of the budget of the United Kingdom for the maintenance of the office of our beloved Queen of all the countries of the commonwealth. He is quite right. There is no contribution made by the Canadian public for the maintenance of the dignity of the monarchy as it exists for the benefit of all the countries of the commonwealth.
In each of the countries of the commonwealth there is a representative of the sovereign. AMENDMENT REGARDING POLL CLERKS AND ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 224, to amend the Canada Elections Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill is very simple. It is based upon a reduction of the force needed to carry out the work of an election on election day, through the elimination of the necessity of having candidates' agents at each poll.
At the present time there is a practice, which is fairly general, by which all candidates-certainly all candidates in opposition to the government party-appoint scrutineers

Canada Elections Act
at each polling place, in order to see that the poll is conducted fairly. In my opinion the majority of that work is unnecessary. Nevertheless, unless there is some machinery set up whereby each polling place can be manned by officers who represent the two opposing political interests, the necessity for those scrutineers, officially known as agents at the polls, will be continued. And no candidate I know of-speaking for myself, I certainly would not-would be prepared to do without having agents at the polls, even though I am reasonably convinced that the polls are operated honestly and according to the act.
The first part of this bill makes an amendment to section 26(4) of the Canada Elections Act, whereby the poll clerk is appointed through the constituency returning officer, but by the right of the candidate representing the party which obtained the highest number of votes at the last preceding federal election, with the proviso that if the highest number of votes was obtained by a candidate supporting the leader of the government, then the candidate obtaining the next highest number of votes would appoint the poll clerk.
This would result in the deputy returning officer being, as he is at the present time, an appointee of the returning officer for the riding, and the poll clerk being an appointee of the candidate representing the party which obtained the highest number of votes, not being the party of the leader of the government.
Under the act at the present time the situation is that the riding returning officers are appointed by order in council.	The
government is responsible for the election, and I think that is perfectly right and proper. The returning officers, however, are appointees of the governor in council, of the leader of the government, and appointees of the party in power. They have the responsibility of choosing the deputy returning officers, who are their appointees	and
consequently are adherents or supporters of the government in power.
The deputy returning officers, in turn, appoint poll clerks; and the poll clerks are therefore, under our present regulations, supporters of the party in power. You have, therefore, a complete chain of the party in power-returning officer to deputy returning officer to poll clerk. The consequence is that any candidate not being a member or a supporter of the party in power, is forced to provide agents at the polls. The providing of agents at polls is one of the great expenses of election day. The average number of polls per constituency in Ontario is 140. Assuming that the candidate pays his agents
[Mr. Adamson.1
a minimum of $5 per day and provides them, as he generally does, with lunch and transportation and other things-

speechtext:
His total expense will run to hundreds of dollars, and in my opinion that is largely unnecessary. The amendment I am proposing to make the poll clerk a member of a party in opposition to the government would eliminate any chance of suspicion that a poll was not adequately carried out. The providing of agents, as I have said, is an expensive matter to the candidate, yet their functions are not of great use. However, a candidate would find it most difficult to dispense with their services. I would not be prepared to advocate that that be done. That is the basic reason for this amendment. I am trying to simplify operations on election day and cut down the expenses of non-government candidates, and make the poll a less congested place than it is at the present time.
Since I introduced this bill I have received a number of communications from people who have been deputy returning officers, who tell me that they agree with the principle of the bill as in their opinion agents at the polls are unnecessary. As I have said, that is one of the unnecessary expenses to which the non-government candidate is put on election day. So much for the basic principle of this amendment.
The term I have used, "leader of the government" is a term used in the office consolidation of the Canadian forces voting regulations in subsection 50, where both the terms "leader of the government" and "leader of the opposition" are mentioned specifically. This bill provides that the representative of the party which led the poll or ran second to the successful candidate can appoint the poll clerks. In other words, in a constituency not held by the Social Credit or the C.C.F. party, where their representatives ran second to the government candidate in 1949, they would be entitled to appoint the poll clerks.
There is also a provision in the bill that if a candidate representing an opposing political interest is not capable of appointing poll clerks the - returning officer shall have the right to do so as he sees fit. There is a time limit on the appointment of poll clerks of two days following nominations, which gives 12 days from nominations in most constituencies and 26 days in others in which the appointment of poll clerks can be made. In other words, poll clerks must be appointed

12 days prior to the date of polling. So much for the first part of the bill.
The second part of the bill deals with advance polls. I find that the Revised Statutes of Canada differ in some particulars from the green election book A-34 as far as advance polls are concerned. The Revised Statutes of Canada, being the official statutes, take precedence over the general election instructions for returning officers. If the point which I now bring to the attention of the house is not cleared up prior to election day there may be some confusion in connection with one or two constituencies.
For instance, in the Revised Statutes of Canada, which we have not as yet received but which I have seen, there is no provision for advance polls at Atikokan, and I think at one or two other places, whereas Atikokan is definitely named in the instructions. It is a simple matter, but it is one which I feel should be cleared up before the general election takes place.
There is one other remark I should like to make with respect to part II of the bill. The township of Etobicoke, which makes up a large part of the constituency of York West, is not mentioned as a place where an advance poll can be established. The townships of Scarborough, York North, York and York East, all being very largely urban municipalities at the present time, have the right to have advance polls, but the township of Etobicoke with a population of over 60,000 does not have that right. I would earnestly request that the house give the township of Etobicoke the right to have advance polls so that it will be treated the same as these other townships in the Toronto metropolitan district.
I realize that introducing a bill to amend a complicated piece of legislation such as the Canada Elections Act at this stage of the session presents some difficulties. However, the amendments I am suggesting are simple in character, and I would ask the government to give earnest consideration to them. In my opinion they would simplify operations at the polls on election day. They would provide for the manning of the polls to be done by two opposing political interests, thus avoiding the necessity of having candidates' agents at the polls and reducing very materially the expense that every candidate who is not a government candidate must assume to carry out the functions which in the name of his party he is bound to carry out on election day.

The hon. member for St. John's West is perfectly right that this item is appearing for the first time in the estimates, and in view of that I think the committee should have a brief explanation. The operation of the ferry service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques is an obligation of Canada under article 32 (1) of the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada. The present ferries and terminal facilities at Port aux Basques form part of the Newfoundland railway and steamship facilities that were acquired by Canada under

the confederation pact. These were entrusted to the Canadian National Railways for operation and management effective April 1, 1949.
The deficits in the operation of the ferry service have been included up to now in the accounts of the Canadian National Railways. In May, 1950, the government, in considering ways and means of relieving the Canadian National Railways of heavy annual deficits, decided that the operation of the ferry service was an obligation of the government as part of the terms of union with Newfoundland, and that the deficits in operation should not be assumed by the railways but should be provided for as a direct obligation of the government. It is proposed that this be done from January 1 of 1952. If my hon. friend will look at the next item in the supplementary estimates he will see that we have a similar item there for the operating deficit of a similar service between the mainland and Prince Edward Island.

I should like to get this
information. There are in this country a large number of people who secured loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation back in 1945 or 1946. At prices prevailing at that time a home could be built for, say, $6,000 or $8,000. During the process of building those homes prices went up terrifically, a fact which left those people in the position of being from $2,000 to $3,000 short of the amount of money required to complete the home. That was owing to inflated prices. Many of them went in debt to the company that furnished the lumber. I myself have had several cases brought to my attention and I have had a great deal of correspondence with the Minister of Resources and Development asking if it was not possible to restore the supplementary loan privilege-
3370	HOUSE OF
Supply-Central Mortgage and Housing which was contained in the act and removed-or if there was not some way in which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could finance that outstanding account by way of a second loan through that organization. There were several cases where the lumber dealer was owed $2,000 or $3,000 and was issuing instructions to have a writ issued against the property holder, and threatening to take the property from him and all that kind of stuff.
The minister and I never got anywhere by way of negotiation. The matter just stood in abeyance. On several occasions he suggested that these people should; go to some other company, get another loan and finance it in that way. However, the people who were affected and for whom I was doing business with the minister were not in a position to do that. Getting another loan meant another $50 a month by way of payment; and they were ordinary people and could not afford it. A lot of people across the country are affected in that way.
I rose this afternoon because of an item that appears in the Journal of this afternoon. It is an account of remarks made to the Rotary Club in Hull by a gentleman named J. C. Paradis, manager of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In his remarks to the Rotary Club in Hull he said that a new policy had been inaugurated by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which would enable homes to be financed directly between the people concerned and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, that it was no longer necessary to farm the money out to the insurance companies.
Without going into a long harangue about the thing, can the minister tell us whether there has been a change in the policy of financing as suggested by this gentleman and whether it is possible now, in the type of case I have just described, to make a direct application to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and perhaps get a new mortgage, including the amount that is owed to the lumber dealer, and have it refinanced by Central Mortgage and Housing?

I shall bring his remarks to the attention of the Minister of Resources and Development, and perhaps he can bring

Crown Liability
respecting the liability of the crown for torts and civil salvage-Mr. Garson-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 8-"Provincial court" defined.
Mr. Chairman, this is a clause which gives jurisdiction to certain provincial courts, limited to what are known as district or county courts, where the maximum jurisdiction is $1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, it is not limited to county courts.
Let us, for example, take the province of British Columbia. I understand that in that province the jurisdiction is given only to the county courts, where the limitation is $1,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is limited as to amount. If the jurisdiction of the county court is not high enough, then it can be taken to the superior court of the province.
But the limit is $1,000, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.

Why is it not made possible for courts of original jurisdiction in each province to deal with these matters? For instance, in British Columbia why should not the supreme court in that province be allowed to deal with the claims?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, for many years the exchequer court has been traditionally the court in which actions between the subject and the crown have been carried on. By reason of the fact that actions from all provinces of Canada between the subject and the crown are carried on in the exchequer court, a uniform jurisprudence has been built up in all of these cases. We think it is desirable that that practice should be continued.
However, it did seem to us desirable that in respect of smaller negligence claims, and the like, where the amounts involved did not exceed $1,000, and where in most provinces it would be possible to have such cases tried in the county or district courts, right in the same community, the subject should be permitted to bring his action in his own county court in his own local district. I am referring to a local district such as the Okanagan or the Kootenay districts of British Columbia.
Therefore we have made this provision. We do believe, however, that where larger amounts are involved and where, as a rule, the more difficult points of law are involved, it is desirable to have actions of that kind brought in the exchequer court, where they will be adjudicated by the same panel of judges in all the provinces of Canada. Since, as my hon. friend knows, the procedure in that court has been considerably simplified

in the last few years and the exchequer court sits in different parts of Canada, the alleged inconvenience of suing in the exchequer court is not as great as at first blush it might appear.
We think that in a statute which is opening up a wide, new field of jurisdiction, as regards causes of action, this is at least the appropriate provision to make.
There is the possibility that the jurisdiction would be extended to the higher courts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Only, I think, if it appeared that there was a need. We are inclined to the view that, with this provision taking care of all the smaller cases in the county courts, there is no particular hardship in suing in the exchequer court, which sits periodically in the different parts of Canada and in which court, I believe, procedure is much simpler than in the average provincial superior court. We think this will work. If it does not work, then I believe we have shown by our conduct in relation to this act that we are quite open-minded and always willing to try to accommodate the public need.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Sections 9 to 13 inclusive agreed to.
On section 14-Rules of court.

Before we proceed to part III may I suggest to the minister that in my submission it would be advisable to have in part II a section providing for discovery and inspection of documents, and for examination for discovery.
I have checked the Ontario statutes, where I find an act respecting proceedings against the crown. In that act section 10 makes provision that the crown may be required to make possible discovery of documents, and to produce documents for inspection. Although couched in different language, there is a similar section in the crown proceedings act of the United Kingdom where, in section 28, provision is also made for examination for discovery.
I suggest it would be very helpful if there were added to the bill a section making provision for the inspection of documents and examination for discovery. May I also suggest that there should be provision in the bill for examination of parties outside the jurisdiction, a point which I consider of some importance. I make my remarks brief, so that we may not be delayed in proceeding to part III.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the experience under the Exchequer Court Act over a period of years had demonstrated that there was great need for discovery in that court, such as my hon.

friend is recommending, then perhaps it might be considered. However, I think my hon. friend will agree that it would be more appropriate to amend the Exchequer Court Act, because if discovery is necessary it should be provided not only for actions of tort covered by the present bill but for all actions taken against the crown in that court. Therefore I think it might be better for us to consider the suggestion which my hon. friend has made in connection with the Exchequer Court Act rather than this bill.
I believe there is provision in all the provinces for discovery under the Exchequer Court Act.
I was not thinking of discovery in the exchequer court, because that is provided for already by the general orders and rules of procedure of that court; and I would refer to rules 129, 130 and 131.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I misunderstood my hon.
friend. I thought he was talking about discovery of documents, not examination for discovery. If my hon. friend's point is that he wishes changes made by this legislation in the rules of procedure of the provincial courts, then I think it would be preferable for us not to change any of the rules of procedure of the provincial courts even if we have the power to do so. I think it would be wise to see how we get along with this bill under the existing rules of procedure in the provincial courts. For my own part, if it was thought desirable to change the rules in the provincial courts I think it would be preferable to communicate with the attorneys general of the provinces to see if they were prepared to change the rules in relation to actions brought under this legislation.
As provision for examination for discovery exists in all provinces there is no need to change the rules of procedure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If it exists in the exchequer court and in all provinces, then why is my hon. friend urging that it should be provided for here?

I feel it would clarify this bill if it were included. We are passing a new statute to apply to all provinces and we would not be infringing upon provincial rights by making discovery a part of this statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid I must differ with my hon. friend. We are dealing with substantive matters in this statute. I think my hon. friend will agree that a provision for examination for discovery is procedural in character. It seems to me that it would be wiser, particularly if he is right when he
Crown Liability
says there is provision already for examination for discovery in the exchequer court and also in the provincial courts, to let these provisions apply and have this statute deal with substantive law, which is what in the main it purports to do.
There may be some doubt as to whether discovery would apply to proceedings under this statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 14 reads:
Except as otherwise provided by this act or the regulations, the rules of practice and procedure of the court in which proceedings under this part are taken apply in those proceedings.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Sections 15 to 21 inclusive agreed to.
On section 22-Service on deputy attorney general.
Mr. Chairman-
More discovery.

It is not more discovery, but we may discover something else. This section reads:
The governor in council may make regulations (a) prescribing rules of practice and procedure in respect of proceedings taken in provincial courts under part II.
I think this fits in with the remarks just made by the Minister of Justice when he said we should not pass laws dealing with procedural matters. I suppose by that he means that he would not want to invade what is recognized as exclusive provincial jurisdiction; yet power is being sought in this very section to prescribe rules of practice and procedure. I have studied the matter very carefully, and I am dubious whether this parliament has the right to prescribe rules of practice and procedure in respect to proceedings taken in provincial courts.
I would appreciate if the minister would point to any authority giving us the right to do that. I submit with due respect that this provision would be ultra vires of the dominion parliament. As a matter of fact there have been cases decided by the privy council with reference to this matter in which procedure has been declared to be within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. I would refer the minister to the case of Attorney General of Quebec v. Reed, reported in 10 Appeal Cases, 141. In that case the privy council was quite clear on the point. I should like to quote from the judgment at page 144 as follows:
One of the things which are to be within the powers of the provincial legislatures-within their exclusive powers-is the administration of justice in the province, including the constitution, main-

Crown Liability
tenance, and organization of provincial courts, and including the procedure in civil matters in the courts.
I think that is applicable to the present situation. There seems to be no doubt that questions of procedure and practice in civil matters in provincial courts are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces and therefore we have no right to pass statutes which invade those exclusive provincial rights. I should like to quote now from Lefroy's "Legislative power in Canada" at page 293, where reference is made to the judgment in McKilligan v. Machar, wherein Killam, J. said:
The provincial legislature has the authority to regulate the administration of justice in the province, including procedure in civil matters in the courts.
I do not take issue with the power of this parliament to pass this legislation, but I have been unable to find any other statute of a similar nature where parliament went as far as it undoubtedly is the intention to go under section 22, namely to prescribe rules of practice and procedure in respect of proceedings taken in provincial courts, including provisions with respect to fees and costs.
In the privy council case which I cited this very question was dealt with inter alia. The Minister of Justice may have some authority, a later decision, to which he can point where this privy council case was overruled. If so I shall be delighted to have the authority on which his law officers are now proceeding; but so far as I have been able to find out I am very dubious whether we have the power to pass such regulations as are provided by section 22. It may be that the minister has some authority. It may be that he has cases. It may be that he will say that the section should go through, but I am sure it will mean an appeal if this parliament attempts to pass regulations to govern the rules of practice and procedure in provincial courts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I thought I understood my hon. friend to suggest a few moments ago that we should prescribe rules of practice with regard to the discovery of documents and the like in provincial courts. But if his actual position is that he is opposing any enactment of this sort in the present bill, I would point out to him, as authorities, that the same thing has been done in the Bankruptcy Act, the Companies Act, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, the Canadian Citizenship Act and the Canada Elections Act, to name only five. I apprehend that as long as the provision which is included in the federal statutes is properly ancillary to the carrying out of the pith and substance of [Mr. Robichaud.j
the act which itself falls within federal jurisdiction, it is intra vires under the Canadian constitution.

Is the position not a little different here? The minister's basic plan is to allow these cases to be tried in the county courts in the same way any other case might be tried in those courts. Why not let the provincial rules applicable to those courts apply? The minister has referred to the Canada Elections Act, the Canadian Citizenship Act and two or three others, but those deal with subjects that do not come under provincial courts in any other way than by virtue of the federal statute. Here we have an entirely different situation in that the minister is opening the door to lawsuits in the provincial county courts. Why not let them be lawsuits of exactly the same type and governed by the same rules as the lawsuits which are brought in those courts at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am in complete agreement with my hon. friend. I indicated a few moments ago that as long as the provincial rules of procedure are adequate there would be no disposition upon our part to change them. But it may be, having regard to the rather wide list of new causes of action which are provided for in the present statute, that in certain provincial procedural statutes there will be a gap that requires to be filled. In that event, and only in that event, would we want to invoke this clause which my hon. friend will see, if he will read it, says that the governor in council "may" make regulations. We do not have to make them, and I can assure him so far as I am concerned as Minister of Justice that we will not make any at all unless it is necessary.
Speaking only for myself, my disposition would be that if we were going to make any such regulations we would certainly write to the provincial attorney general and confer with him as to the necessity. Perhaps it would be possible for him to change his own rules to accommodate the point we had in mind. In other words, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has suggested we would very much prefer, for obvious reasons, that in any proceedings taken in provincial courts under this present statute we should abide by the rules of those provincial courts.

Why not delete clause (a) and depend on clause (e) to meet that situation? It is wide enough to cover anything that is required. Then you get away from the very broad wording of clause (a) which in effect says that the governor in council can step in and prescribe rules for the county courts in

British Columbia, Ontario or anywhere else. I think that is an unnecessarily wide provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the light of the explanation I have just given surely there is no harm, when we are bringing in a wide list of new causes of action against the crown that have not been used before and to which the provincial rules may not be closely applicable, in taking this power which we may not and which I hope we shall not exercise. It is there if we require it. If we do not require it we certainly will not use it. I do not see how it can possibly do any harm.
The statute does not set up any new causes of action. All it does is to make the crown subject to certain causes of action that have been in existence for a long time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course it all depends upon how one looks at it, but I do suggest to my hon. friend that there are a number of sets of facts which arise in Canada in which the crown, upon the passage of the bill, would be involved as defendant. In each of these cases there is no cause of action now. Hence, with all deference, I would suggest that we are creating causes of action.
But they are similar to causes of action against private individuals.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes, but never against the crown until the present time.

The minister has sought to place me in a dilemma by making reference to my previous remarks concerning the advisability of embodying in the statute provisions for the discovery and inspection of documents. But may I say to the minister that when 1 made my first suggestion before we got through with part II I did so with the intention of finding out exactly what the minister's position was in regard to my suggestion. I submit now that by passing the regulations provided for in section 22 the minister will, in my humble submission, certainly be invading the exclusive rights of the provinces to prescribe rules and regulations as far as practice, procedure and other matters are concerned.

Section agreed to.
Sections 23 to 25 inclusive agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We shall now revert to section 4 which was allowed to stand. Hon. members will recall that subsection 4 of clause 4 was allowed to stand for the purpose of possibly moving an amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yesterday when this clause was before the committee the hon. member

for Eglinton referred, as hon. members will recall, to the provisions of what we take to be the Ontario municipal act calling for the giving of notice in cases of claims against municipalities. He suggested, if I understood him correctly, that the provision which was applicable in the province of Ontario might be made applicable here rather than the wording which we have employed. We have examined the provision in question. I have no hesitation, Mr. Chairman, in accepting it.
I might suggest that we add a new subclause to clause 4 of this bill in the terms of the Ontario section, and then have it passed. Might I read the Ontario section:
In the case of the death of the person injured, failure to give notice shall not be a bar to the action and except where the injury was caused by snow or ice upon a sidewalk, failure to give or insufficiency of the notice shall not be a bar to the action, if the court or judge before whom the action is tried is of the opinion that the corporation in its defence was not prejudiced by the want or insufficiency of the notice, and that to bar the action would be an injustice, notwithstanding that reasonable excuse for the want or insufficiency of the notice is not established.
In other words the claimant, even although he cannot establish a reasonable excuse for not having given the notice, will nevertheless have a claim if the court or judge before whom the action is tried is of the opinion that the corporation, in its defence-in our case it would be the federal crown-was not prejudiced by the want or insufficiency of the notice, and that to bar the action would be an injustice. Might I suggest that we have that put into the form of a new subclause to clause 4 of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, may I suggest to the minister that he delete that exception which refers to snow or ice. I doubt very much whether that provision is in the Ontario statute. Of course I do not know whether or not it is, but it does seem to be an unnecessary restriction. Why not leave it to the judge in any case to decide whether or not relief should be given against the failure to give notice within seven days?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will agree that if the judge is going to decide something, you have to give him some criteria upon which to base his decision. The criterion which is stated here is that the crown has not been prejudiced in its defence by the failure to give that notice within the prescribed period. What we are doing here is really meeting my hon. friend's view that he has just expressed. It is hardly fair to the judge to leave it completely in his discretion. He has to have some standard upon which he can judge whether or not it is proper or not to grant the relief.

Crown Liability

Why not leave it to the judge instead of putting in the exception for snow or ice? As I pointed out to the minister last evening, I had a person come in to see me whose wife had been injured because of the ice on the sidewalk in front of the immigration office at the border below Vancouver. The wife was quite seriously hurt, and the husband was very worried about her. She was taken to hospital and there was great concern about her. If I remember correctly this man did not come to the office until one week had elapsed, so that under this provision the judge would have no power to exempt him from the provision requiring the seven days' notice because the wording refers to snow and ice. I think the matter should be left to the discretion of the judge. Surely we can trust our judiciary that far, without saying that when the accident was caused by snow or ice they have no right to give further time. I am sure the Prime Minister would agree that that is an unnecessary restriction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This section was before the committee yesterday, and the hon. member for Eglinton took exception to the section upon the ground that there was no saving subsection such as the one I have just quoted which would protect the claimant in cases such as the one to which my hon. friend has just referred. The hon. member for Eglinton referred to this provision in the Ontario statute. I understood him to say that he regarded that as something which should be in this bill. As I have said, in an endeavour to meet the views of the opposition in a reasonable way, we have examined the Ontario section and we are offering to adopt it.
Now the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra says he wants to improve on the Ontario section to some extent. I wonder if we might not leave the matter as it is. If any difficulty develops under it, then we could consider amending it again. From the fact that this provision has been in the Ontario act I would assume that it must have been found to be fairly satisfactory or there would have been public opinion in favour of changing it.

The hon. member for Eglinton did not disagree with me last night at all. We were both asking that the exception of an accident arising from snow or ice be deleted. No suggestion was made by the hon. member for Eglinton that he agreed there might be such an exception. I would suggest that we give the trial judge the right to decide whether or not notice has been given within a reasonable time, rather than putting in that restriction against the type of claim 
arising from snow or ice. I have given the minister one example which I have had in my own practice where it would be absolutely unfair to deny these people the right to claim because they did not file within the seven days. All I am asking is that the minister take out the words excepting snow and ice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend is well aware of the reason for their inclusion in the Ontario statute or in similar statutes of that nature. Where the damage arises from a condition of snow or ice, unless the defendant is acquainted with the condition which is alleged to have caused the injury the defendant has no opportunity at all of examining what is essentially an ephemeral condition. It is gone in a short time. Then the defendant is entirely at the mercy of the plaintiff as to what the condition was. The condition has passed away, and the defendant is handicapped in making his defence.
I am sure the provision in the Ontario statute was put there not because of any unfairness on the part of the Ontario legislature or the Ontario municipalities, but because the need for it in cases of that kind was recognized. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that the hon. member for Eglinton, like himself, was not at all enthusiastic over this provision about snow and ice. As I understood it, though, he did not have this section with him. He was advocating that we consider it. We have looked it up, and we are quite prepared to adopt it to meet the suggestion he made.

You see, the case I have mentioned could have been decided by a judge because in that case an immigration officer was right there and knew about the accident within a minute after it happened. The crown would not have been prejudiced in any way if it had not had notice within seven days. Now, this case would come before a judge, and the judge would say, "Well, the crown has not suffered because notice was not given within the seven days." He would allow the suit to continue. If the minister puts in this restriction, this suit is automatically wiped out because it arises out of snow and ice. I suggest that is going too far.
I would ask the minister to take out those words and leave it to the trial judge to decide in every case.
May I ask the minister the length of notice required under the Ontario municipal act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the Ontario municipal act it is seven days.

The hon. member for Eglinton after having proposed this saving clause

also said this, and I am quoting from page 3335 of Hansard:
I would urge on the minister that even with such a saving provision, a period of seven days is still too short.
If the only obsession in the minister's mind now is the possibility of a case arising from slippery conditions due to snow or ice, my submission would be just the contrary. By this I mean that seven days is too long. You should make it seven hours if that is the only thing in the way. I am certainly in accord with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra to eliminate this notice in the case of snow and ice, because in my province if it is seven days or even seven months, it is all right; but in some places, for slippery conditions, seven days is far too long. Why not eliminate the snow and ice condition entirely in the proposed amending subsection?

Surely the hon. member for Gloucester has exploded the unreasonableness of the exception for snow and ice because, as he says, if you have conditions of snow and ice, seven days is far too long, exactly as he says. I think he shows the unreasonableness of the exception.
The unreasonableness of asking to accept what is in the Ontario legislation?
We have a high opinion of Ontario, but they are not always perfect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are too many sea lawyers around here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With great deference to my hon. friends on the opposite side who have just spoken, I suggest that in matters of this kind great consideration should be given to the experience of municipal administrators over a period of years. These provisions that appear in municipal statutes do not get there because some person has had an abstract idea. They get there because they are based upon the experience of the municipalities over the years.
What my hon. friends-I think somewhat unreasonably-are asking is that in a statute which is creating a wide list of new causes of action against the crown we should, without any experience upon which to base our provision in the statutes, adopt a wording which is much more onerous upon the crown than that which is provided by the Ontario legislature for the municipalities of that province. I think where we are making the considerable concessions that are being made in this statute, it is surely reasonable that

we should adopt in this section the same sort of provision which has prevailed in the Ontario statutes for some years and apparently has been found to be consonant with public opinion generally.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (for the Minister of Fisheries) moved
