subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR HIGH SEAS FISHERIES
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure providing for the approval and confirmation of the international convention for the high seas fisheries of the north Pacific ocean, signed by Canada, the United States and Japan, in Tokyo, on the 9th of May, 1952, and for carrying out Canada's obligations under the convention.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. Watson MacNaughl (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR HIGH SEAS FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the international convention for the high seas fisheries of the north Pacific ocean was drafted at a tripartite fisheries convention held in Tokyo in the fall of 1951. This conference was attended by delegations representing the governments of Canada, Japan and the United States.
The Canadian delegation was made up of the recent minister of fisheries, Hon. Mr. Mayhew, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite); the deputy minister of fisheries, Mr. Bates; the legal adviser of the Department of Fisheries, Mr. Ozere; a representative from the external affairs department, Mr. Menzies; John L. Hart, director of the Pacific biological station; and John M. Buchanan, representing the fishing industry of British Columbia. Japan was given an ad hoc sovereignty by the supreme command of the allied forces for the purposes of negotiating the convention. Upon the coming into force of the Japanese peace treaty, the convention was signed on behalf of the three governments on May 9, 1952.
The convention is made in respect of fishing in the high seas of the North Pacific ocean. Territorial waters are excepted and claims to territorial waters unaffected.
The principal provisions of the convention relate to agreement on the part of each of the three contracting parties to abstain from fishing in the high seas outside the territorial waters for any stocks of fish which are (a) under scientific management, (b) legal regulation, and (c) fully exploited by one or two of the contracting parties. Under these provisions Japan immediately agreed to abstain from fishing for salmon, halibut and herring on
[The Chairman.]

this side of the Pacific ocean. These three species constitute the backbone of the fishing industry in British Columbia. We have agreed to abstain from fishing for red salmon in certain areas of the Bering sea, where our fishermen have never conducted any fishing operations, and where the United States have developed the salmon fishery without our participation.
By way of exception to these general principles, under which each of the parties agreed to abstain from exploiting the resources conserved and developed by one or two of the other parties, the treaty recognizes that, because of intermingling of fish and fishing operations, and because of joint conservation programs, neither Canada nor the United States would be asked to abstain from the exploitation of the fishery resources on this side of the Pacific from the gulf of Alaska southward. This exception is of particular interest to Canada, since our fishermen have not historically established fishing operations along the greatest part of the coast of the United States, including Alaska; whereas United States' fishermen have been fishing in the high seas off our territorial waters in many areas along the coast of British Columbia, and therefore could not be asked to abstain because of this historic exploitation.
Subject to these exceptions, any other stock of fish that in the future meets with the three conditions of full exploitation, scientific management and legal regulation may be included in the annex of the treaty, and the party or parties which have not participated in this exploitation may be asked to abstain from future exploitation.
The treaty provides for the establishment of a commission composed of representatives of the three countries, whose functions will include determination of whether any stock of fish qualifies for abstention under the principles of the convention. The commission would also decide whether any joint conservation measures are required in respect of any stock of fish exploited by two or all of the contracting parties. In case only two countries are interested in a certain fishery, the representatives of the two countries concerned would alone make the necessary recommendations; otherwise the recommendations of the commission are to be unanimous.
The commission has no regulatory powers, but only the power of making recommendations which can only become effective if agreed to by the governments of the three countries. Each government is to pay the expenses incurred by its national section. Joint expenses are to be paid in the form and proportion recommended by the commission

and approved by the three governments. Search and arrest of fishing vessels on the high seas, operating contrary to the provisions of the convention, are agreed to. Such vessels when seized are to be turned over to the country to which they belong for trial and punishment. This procedure is in line with the procedure now provided for in our two treaties with the United States on salmon and halibut.
The convention will enter into force on the day of exchange of ratification and will remain in force for ten years, and thereafter one year from the day on which any party gives notice of termination. The treaty has already been ratified by the government of the United States and approved by the diet of Japan, and it is thought desirable that it should be ratified by the government of Canada as soon as possible.
By a protocol to the convention the commission shall, as soon as possible after its establishment, investigate the waters of the convention area to determine if there are areas in which salmon of United States, Canadian and Asiatic origin intermingle, and recommend suitable lines of demarcation in place of the provisional line now agreed upon.
The convention was referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries for study. The committee on June 10, 1952 unanimously recommended that the House of Commons approve the convention. Implementing legislation will be required to carry out Canada's obligation under the convention. This resolution envisages such implementing legislation.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR HIGH SEAS FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the parliamentary assistant has said, this convention was examined carefully in the standing committee on marine and fisheries a year ago. It is therefore not the intention to have a protracted debate at the resolution stage here. But in view of a certain amount of misunderstanding which existed on the west coast, and a good deal of controversy which took place, I would appreciate the opportunity of making a few remarks on this subject.
It was considered by many people that it would have been preferable to have included this convention in the general peace treaty, but we learned in the committee that that was not considered either practicable or desirable when the Japanese peace treaty was being drawn up at San Francisco, and the committee accepted the explanations which were then given. As a result of the impossibility of the inclusion of special fishery clauses in the general peace treaty, this tripartite treaty or convention was drawn up.
North Pacific Fishery
I understand that the convention is aimed in general terms at the conservation of fisheries resources in a very large area of the Pacific ocean, with special treatment for a limited period of time, namely eleven years and one day, or longer, to fisheries which are being fully exploited and are already subject to conservation methods, as has just now been described by the parliamentary assistant.
Japan is excluded, in certain sections of the high seas off the coast of the United States territory of Alaska and British Columbia, from fishing salmon, herring and halibut for the period described. Canada and Japan have agreed to abstain from fishing salmon which originates in the waters of the rivers of Alaska flowing into the Bering sea.
One unique point regarding the fisheries on the west coast is that, historically, Canada and the United States have been the only powers which have fished in the high seas off the west coast of Canada. I do not think there is any recorded incident in which a foreign fishing vessel, other than those of the United States, has fished off the west coast of Canada. Of course, in the past Japanese fishing vessels have been off the Alaska coast, in the Bering sea. But fear exists among many people in the industry that this immunity may not last forever and that, owing to the rapid development in fishing vessels, including the increase in their size, it may be that foreign fishing fleets will come to the high seas off the coast of British Columbia in the not too distant future.
It is known that at the present time Japan has trawlers to a gross tonnage of 664 tons, and that they have modern steel clippers that they use in their fishing industry. But Japan is not the only country developing fishing fleets ranging over the ocean for thousands of miles, and so there is the fear that not only may Japanese fishing fleets come off our coasts, but also the fishing fleets of other nations who border on the Pacific ocean.
For many years we have spent a great deal of money and effort in the conservation of our fish. I say "our" fish because I mean our Canadian fish, our British Columbia fish, the fish born and bred hundreds of miles up the rivers of my province. And then the salmon, having spawned, work down the rivers and pass out through our territorial waters into the high seas. In the majority of cases they have to pass through waters surrounded by Canadian territory for some considerable distance before they actually get into the ocean. Naturally I refer to such passages as the strait of Juan de Fuca and Hecate strait between the Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland of British Columbia.

North Pacific Fishery
I think it is appropriate at the moment to call attention to the importance of the fishing industry to the Japanese nation, as it is indicative of her interest in that industry not only at the present time hut also in years to come. In pre-war days-and I am referring to the time before world war II-the Japanese fleet was catching from 3 to 5 million tons of fish each year, and that country was exporting about a million tons. During the war, of course, her fishing activities were very much restricted, and were confined to fishing close to the islands of Japan. Her export trade was completely cut off.
After the war, beginning in 1951, although still under certain restrictions placed upon her by the occupying powers Japan did carry out extensive fishing operations. She was encouraged to do so. Her total catch that year was 3,500,000 tons. In 1952 she increased that catch by at least 20 per cent. I have here a report from World Fishing, a trade magazine of the United Kingdom dealing with fishing, which has this to say about Japanese endeavours at the present time:
Japan is apparently losing little time in making use ol her new fishing freedom. Plans reported to be under consideration for 1953 include five or six salmon expeditions involving 200 catchers, further whaling operations, a crab expedition, a trawling venture (chiefly for cod) employing five boats and1 a fish carrier, and a fish-meal factory ship expedition with 25 catchers.
Japan is already looking far afield for possible extensions to her fishery activities.
It is the fear of the extension of those fishing activities by Japan and by other countries that looms over the fishermen of British Columbia. They have expressed considerable disappointment that an opportunity was not taken, when the convention was prepared, of defining in article I more clearly what our territorial waters are, because this treaty deals with the high seas and of course the high seas come right up to where our territorial waters may be.
In Scott's "Law and Customs of the Seas", which is a textbook of the Royal Canadian Navy, navigable waters of the world are divided into internal waters, territorial waters and the high seas. This classification begins on the landward side and requires of course two lines, one demarking the division between internal and territorial waters, and the other defining the line between territorial waters and the high seas. Quite obviously the internal waters of a state comprise all those waters, salt or fresh, which lie on the landward side of the line dividing the internal waters from the territorial waters. This will include all rivers, fresh lakes, harbours and the like.
A well-known authority, Mr. V. K. Johnston, who wrote a quite complete article in the British Year Book of International Law a few years ago, sets out the claims of Canada to certain waters, particularly Hudson bay. The waters of Hudson bay are controlled by Canada, and Canada has laid claim for many centuries to those waters as being internal waters of Canada. That claim has been established in the statutes of Canada. Other countries have done the same. Japan had claimed the Inland sea as her own internal waters. Russia has claimed the White sea. The United States has claimed Chesapeake bay. Those are just some examples of the claims that have been made to internal waters.
Many plans have been suggested for the drawing of a base line to indicate the territorial waters. As far as Hudson bay is concerned, that bay is 1,000 miles long by about 600 miles wide. This huge expanse of water is joined to the Atlantic ocean by Hudson strait, another stretch of water some 500 miles long and 46 miles wide. In 1906 the government of Canada placed a measure upon the statute books claiming the waters of Hudson bay to be territorial waters of Canada.
I cite that as an instance of what Canada has done in the past in the way of claiming a wide stretch of salt water which is connected to the Atlantic ocean. On the west coast we have not had the continued incidents of foreign countries fishing off our coast, but we feel that the time has come when steps should be taken to declare that the waters between the Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland, through which fish born in the waters of British Columbia must pass to get to the Pacific ocean, should be declared to be territorial or internal waters.
We believe that that can be done now, and we regret that it was not included in this convention. There should have been a clear definition claiming for all time, not just for ten or eleven years, that Hecate strait constituted territorial waters of Canada and that Japan should be prohibited for all time from fishing for salmon, herring, halibut or any other fish in those Canadian waters.
We recognize the historic right of the United States to fish there. For years United States fishermen have been fishing in these waters and have observed and will continue to observe the conservation regulations which we have laid down for the protection of our fish. But that does not necessarily apply to Japan or other countries bordering on the Pacific ocean. We feel that this convention should have afforded an opportunity

to establish those waters as Canadian territorial waters. Even if that were not done, we feel that for all time there should have been a claim made by Canada to preserve the salmon, halibut, herring and other fish that inhabit those waters.
It is not unusual for countries to claim fishing preserves or rights over certain waters of the high seas outside of their own territorial waters. For instance, the United Kingdom has laid claim to the oyster beds in St. George's channel, which are more than 20 miles from the coast. The United Kingdom claims that she has certain fishing rights there and she exercises certain regulations over the breeding and harvesting of those oysters. In the same way sponge fisheries off the Tunisian coast are specially protected although they are well outside territorial waters. Similarly, fishing and conservation regulations have been made by Mexico and some of the South American republics.
I am not going into the question of how a base line should be drawn, but we do have the example of Norway. That nation recently made the decision to draw a base line from point to point, some points being 40 miles distant. These fixed points were on headlands, small islands and rocks stretching up the whole length of the west coast of Norway. We feel it is high time that steps were taken to declare Hecate strait as Canadian waters, and to say that we have the right to conserve our fish in those waters.
I understand that a committee has been set up and is going into the whole problem, and also that this matter will be referred to a committee of the United Nations which is discussing the question of territorial waters. I repeat that we regret that opportunity was not taken when this convention was drawn to define clearly where our territorial waters were on the west coast and establish once and for all our right to the fish which breed in Canadian waters and pass through Hecate strait and other waters surrounded either by the shores of the mainland of Canada or islands off the west coast.
If Canada can lay claim to the vast area of Hudson bay, surely she has the right to claim Hecate strait which is also surrounded by Canadian territory. Hecate strait is an insignificant piece of water when its size is compared with Hudson bay and Hudson strait. The strait is not more than 30 or 40 miles wide at the widest point between the mainland and the Queen Charlotte islands.
Those are the objections we have to this convention. We do not feel that we can go so far as to object to its ratification, but we do urge that the committee which has been set up to deal with territorial waters should
Post Office Act
proceed with the utmost dispatch and try to reach an agreement with the other countries concerned so that now, before it is too late, before foreign fishing fleets come off our shores, all nations will know that Canada claims that sheet of water.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Mr. Fournier, Hull (for Mr. Sinclair) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 293, to implement the international convention for the high seas fisheries of the north Pacific ocean.

I am not a member of this committee but, from reading this bill, I want to say that it is a step in the right direction for the rural mail carriers of Canada. Items this bill will cover have come to my attention time and time again in connection with various rural mail carriers throughout my part of the country in connection with the money they were going to receive.
If they were not receiving an adequate sum of money for the services rendered to the people in that part of the country, and if they felt that was the case, they would write to the Post Office Department, and in most cases they would have to call for new tenders. Then some person would proceed to tender who had no conception of the work involved, and he might be awarded the contract because he was able to deliver a bond or he was able to show that he had proper equipment to carry on the job. But at the end of six months or three months that man would realize that he was going to go bankrupt if he continued at that price, and then he would throw up the contract. In the meantime the man who had asked for a reasonable sum of money would have been upset and would have turned to another vocation in order to provide his livelihood. The net result would be that the recipients of the mail, the people of this country who are looking for mail delivery, would be upset and would not get the mail service to which they were entitled.
From reading this act I think I can say there is no doubt about it that it is one step in the right direction-and I want to compliment the committee-so that our mail carriers will probably get somewhere near an adequate remuneration for the services they render to the people of Canada. Further steps can be taken and improvements can be made, but definitely this bill provides for an improvement in the conditions under which these men have been working, and I am glad to see it.

Having gone over the various proposals that have been made from time to time, I must confess that I am practically driven back to the position that I do not know any other way out at the moment than that which the bill has provided.
It may be that there are other ways out, but I do not know of any. You cannot put them on a civil service basis because they will not go on it. They do not perhaps want to rout out a lot of them who are there now. You cannot leave them on a tender basis without some kind of elasticity or latitude because it is a throat-cutting job with a great many people and the result is that that is where much of the injustice has arisen. While I have been arguing and would continue to argue that we have to watch out that we do not get this on a straight patronage basis, one of the things that was interesting to me when the debate took place previously was an observation made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. I must confess that I thought there was quite a bit in what he said.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext: There always is.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext: I would not have thought it would be necessary to mention that. You would almost think it was the exception to the rule, but I would not agree with you on that.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext:
I was just helping you out.

Post Office Act

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext:
As far as I can see, this seems about the best that can be done, at least for the time being, with regard to giving them some elasticity and some satisfaction in knowing that when they are too low in price, are not able to make any money, and are running on starvation rates, the minister can do something for them. That is really the agreeable part of it. It may be that we shall run into many difficulties with this new system. I do not know; but at least it is important that we try it out to see if it will work.
At the same time I should like to caution the minister. He will have to watch that it does not get into the position where it is a straight patronage matter on rural mail routes, not only for the sake of party advantage to anybody but for the sake of the Postmaster General himself. He would be put in a very invidious position if it got into that situation. I am thinking too of the deputy postmaster general, whom we must always have in mind. In any event, it does seem to me that it is deserving at least of a trial, and that is why I rise to endorse it. I do not know of any other way out. If I did I would be presenting it to the committee just now.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext:
Section 2 reads:
Where more than one tender has been received, the contract shall be awarded to the lowest tenderer who has offered sufficient security for the faithful performance of the contract, unless the Postmaster General is satisfied that it is not in the public interest to accept the lowest tender . . .
There is a clause in the Post Office Act that says practically the same thing, namely that the Postmaster General need not give the job to a certain fellow. He may be the top man in the competition for a post office job or even for the job as courier, but the Postmaster General need not give him that job. There is a clause in the act which says "for cause". This has happened twice in my riding, and it was absolutely nothing but the barest unadulterated patronage that was used in both cases. I do not blame the deputy postmaster general, because in one instance he was not in town. He was away on his holidays.

speechtext: My hon. friend may obtain all the information he wants. He may also ask for the production of papers, that is, papers that are not considered confidential.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext: I am glad to hear that, because that is quite a change from your predecessor.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext: I should like to ask a question on this clause. If the Postmaster General finds that one man's route is 15 miles and he is getting $1,000 and the next fellow has a mail route of 24 miles and is getting only $800, will he immediately say that this is not fair and raise him to $2,400.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext: That is precisely the purpose of the bill. The purpose of the bill is to do away with unfairness, to see that people who are suffering injustices get just treatment.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext: Don't start at the lowest tender, because these people have been robbed all their lives; they have been working for nothing. I should like to have some assurance that you will start at the highest-paid ones and work from there, and not from the lowest ones and work up.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext:
I might satisfy my hon. friend by saying that the readjustment will be made in an objective way after we have received information from the Department of Labour and from our officers in the field. I do not want to give all the details, but instead of readjusting arbitrarily we shall find out what is paid for

comparable services in the same area and we shall pay an adequate remuneration to the contractors.

speechtext: Comparable services in something else besides driving the mail?

speakerposition: Postmaster General

speechtext: Driving the mail and driving something else, perhaps. Similar work might satisfy my hon. friend.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext: Where you are increasing the amount paid to a lot of these men who have been using worn-out equipment, will the department see to it that their equipment is brought up to the standards necessary?

speechtext:
We always look at all the angles. Public interest was mentioned. That is one way of expressing what we are looking for. We want to see that the taxpayers of this country receive good service, and we want the man who is giving the service to be paid adequately. To achieve that we are looking at the security, the solvency of the men and the equipment, and a comparison of the routes, the number of boxes, the length of the routes; and all these considerations will be looked into and taken into consideration in the decision we are going to make.
